# 1. Introduction

## Motivation

Floods in the Colorado Rockies originate from at least three distinct
hydrometeorological mechanisms: warm-season convective rainfall, spring snowmelt
driven by solar radiation, and rain-on-snow (ROS) events where precipitation
falls onto a melting snowpack and both fluxes combine to generate runoff. These
mechanisms produce flood peaks with systematically different statistical
characteristics. Extreme snowmelt floods are constrained by the available snow
water equivalent, which limits upper-tail magnitudes, while convective rainfall
events are not subject to the same physical bound and can generate more extreme
short-duration peaks. Rain-on-snow events compound both fluxes and may produce
the most extreme floods of all in high-elevation basins with large seasonal
snowpacks.

Classical flood frequency analysis (FFA) treats all peaks as exchangeable
draws from a single population and fits a single distribution to the merged
record. When flood-generating mechanisms are systematically different, this
aggregation conflates populations with different distributional properties,
biasing both the fitted distribution and the resulting quantile estimates. The
mixture FFA framework of Yu et al. (2022) addresses this by fitting separate
distributions to peaks of each process type and constructing a mixture survival
function whose component CDFs are multiplied. The resulting mixture curve is
formally motivated by the assumption that a flood exceeding a given level must
arise from one of the contributing processes, and that exceedance by each
process is approximately independent conditional on flood type.

This report documents the classification and FFA pipeline developed for the
CoWC FY26 Enhanced Impacts project, following the Yu et al. (2022) framework.
It describes the three classification methods implemented, the methodological
decisions made during development, and the key results.

## Study Area and Site Selection

The study covers Colorado streamgages from the GAGES-II dataset, including both
reference (minimally disturbed) and non-reference sites. Site metadata —
including drainage area, mean basin elevation, upstream dam storage, and
GAGES-II classification — were assembled from the standard GAGES-II attribute
tables. Sites were flagged as regulated if upstream normal storage exceeded
1,000 acre-feet (1.233 Mm³), following the criterion used by Davenport et al.
(2020). Of the 206 Colorado sites in the dataset, 63 are unregulated and are
the primary sample for FFA. The full 206-site fleet is used for classification
and diagnostic analysis.

## Data

**USGS discharge.** Daily maximum discharge was derived from USGS unit
(15-minute) streamflow data accessed via the USGS Water Data API using the
`dataRetrieval` R package. Peaks over threshold (POT) were identified using a
per-site threshold equal to the 50th percentile of the daily maximum flow
record, which also serves as the GPD location parameter $\mu$ in downstream
frequency fitting following Yu et al. (2022). Peaks were declustered using the
minimum time-separation criterion from Livneh et al. (2024):
$\theta = 5 + \ln(1.6092 \cdot A)$ days, where $A$ is drainage area in km².
The output contains approximately 21,000 distinct peaks across all 206 sites.

**WLDAS hydrometeorological drivers.** Antecedent rainfall and snowmelt were
obtained from the Western Land Data Assimilation System (WLDAS), a Noah-MP
land surface model product at 0.01° (~1 km) spatial resolution. Daily NetCDF
files were processed using `exactextractr`, extracting basin-mean values for
rainfall flux, snowfall flux, snowmelt flux (from the snowmelt parameterization
in Noah-MP), and snow water equivalent (SWE). Flux variables were converted from
kg m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ to mm/day. Outputs were written as date-partitioned
Parquet files and processed into 60-day accumulation curves for each POT peak.

\newpage

# 2. Classification Approaches Overview

Three flood classification methods were implemented and compared. Each method
takes the same input — basin-averaged WLDAS antecedent fluxes over a per-peak
antecedent window — and assigns each POT peak to one or more flood types.

The **Depth threshold method** (Script 6a) applies the absolute accumulation
thresholds of Davenport et al. (2020) to 8-day antecedent totals of rainfall and
snowmelt flux. Peaks are assigned to Rainfall, Snowmelt, Rain-on-Snow, or
Unclassified based on whether each flux exceeds 10 mm or falls below 5 mm over
the fixed window. This method is the primary baseline from the literature and
provides direct comparability with prior work on the Colorado River basin.

The **Rain fraction (3-class) method** (Script 6b) replaces raw accumulation
totals with a scale-invariant rain fraction metric (`rain_frac`) computed over a
site-specific antecedent window derived from the basin's characteristic response
time. Classification uses two thresholds applied sequentially: peaks with
`rain_frac >= 0.99` are assigned to Rainfall; remaining mixed events are split at
the population-level median rain fraction (MIXED_SPLIT = 0.2979) into Snowmelt
(below) and Rain-on-Snow (above). The Snowmelt and Rain-on-Snow labels are
operationally defined — they describe position in the mixed-event rain fraction
distribution, not direct physical process attribution. This method is the primary
classification for FFA.

The **Rain fraction (2-class) method** is a downstream remap produced in Script 7
that collapses the Snowmelt and Rain-on-Snow classes from the 3-class output into
a single Non-Rainfall class, yielding a two-type (Rainfall, Non-Rainfall)
classification. It provides a structural sensitivity check: if the boundary
between Snowmelt and Rain-on-Snow within the mixed-event pool does not
meaningfully differentiate upper-tail flood magnitudes, the 2-class and 3-class
mixture curves should converge.

All three methods apply the same Yu et al. (2022) minimum sample size filters
(MIN_TYPE_SAMPLE = 20, MIN_SINGLE_SAMPLE = 25) and the same single-sample
selection protocol, so differences in FFA output reflect classification
structure rather than downstream analytical choices.

\newpage

# 3. Fixed Depth Threshold Classification

## 3.1 Method Description

The Davenport et al. (2020) method classifies POT peaks using the total
accumulated rainfall and snowmelt over a fixed 8-day antecedent window
preceding each peak. The thresholds were calibrated using station data from the
Colorado River basin and are intended to capture the dominant hydrometeorological
forcing type. A peak is assigned to Snowmelt if antecedent snowmelt accumulation
exceeds 10 mm and antecedent rainfall falls below 5 mm; to Rainfall if
antecedent rainfall exceeds 10 mm and snowmelt falls below 5 mm; and to
Rain-on-Snow if both fluxes exceed 5 mm simultaneously. Peaks that do not meet
any of these criteria — including peaks with ambiguous intermediate signals or
insufficient WLDAS coverage — are classified as Unclassified.

The fixed 8-day window was chosen to capture the precipitation-to-runoff lag
for typical western US watersheds. However, hydrologic response time scales vary
systematically with basin size: small headwater catchments respond within hours,
while large basins may require many days for a precipitation signal to propagate
to the outlet. The Livneh et al. (2024) peak independence criterion encodes this
scaling explicitly as $\theta = 5 + \ln(1.6092 \cdot A)$, where $A$ is drainage
area in km². Across Colorado GAGES-II sites, $\theta$ ranges from roughly 8 to
17 days, with most sites between 10 and 15 days. For sites where $\theta > 8$,
the Davenport 8-day window discards antecedent forcing information that the
independence criterion itself identifies as hydrologically relevant.

## 3.2 Decision Tree

```{r davenport-flowchart, fig.cap = "Decision tree for the Davenport et al. (2020) fixed depth threshold classification. Threshold values (5 mm and 10 mm) apply to total accumulated flux over an 8-day antecedent window."}

## 3.3 Rationale for Retaining Literature Thresholds

The thresholds of Davenport et al. (2020) are well-established in the Colorado
basin literature and were derived from a principled analysis of co-occurrence
patterns in the WLDAS record. They reproduce a reasonable classification
composition across Colorado sites, with snowmelt-dominated events concentrated
in high-elevation basins and rainfall events more common at lower elevations —
consistent with the known climatological structure of the region.

A data-driven approach to threshold selection is not viable here for a
fundamental physical reason: rainfall-dominated peaks and snowmelt-dominated
peaks occur in hydrologically distinct basin states (saturated versus frozen
soils, respectively), and their runoff ratios reflect entirely different
infiltration regimes. Optimizing boundaries to equalize cross-type runoff ratios
would conflate two physically distinct processes rather than improve
classification fidelity. The Davenport thresholds are therefore retained without
modification in Script 6a.

\newpage

# 4. Rain Fraction Classification

## 4.1 Method Description

The rain fraction classification (Script 6b) replaces the Davenport fixed
accumulation thresholds with a scale-invariant feature — the weighted rain
fraction (`rain_frac`) — computed over a site-specific antecedent window. The
antecedent window length for each site is set equal to the Livneh et al. (2024)
peak-independence criterion $\theta = \lceil 5 + \ln(1.6092 \cdot A) \rceil$
days (the `search_radius` parameter), so that the window defining event
independence also defines the window over which antecedent forcing is
accumulated.

The rain fraction is defined as:

$$\text{rain\_frac} = \frac{\sum_{d=1}^{W} \tilde{r}_d}{\sum_{d=1}^{W} (\tilde{r}_d + \tilde{m}_d)}$$

where $W$ is `search_radius`, and $\tilde{r}_d$, $\tilde{m}_d$ are rainfall and
snowmelt flux on day $d$ set to zero if below a noise floor of 0.1 mm/day. Days
where both fluxes fall below the noise floor contribute nothing to either the
numerator or denominator. The resulting metric is bounded on $[0, 1]$ and
comparable across basins regardless of climatological flux magnitude.

Classification rules are applied in the following order:

1. **Unclassified**: fewer than 90% of `search_radius` days have WLDAS data, or
   `rain_frac` is undefined (zero total antecedent flux after noise-floor
   removal).
2. **Rainfall**: `rain_frac >= RAIN_FRAC_THRESH` (= 0.99). The tolerance below
   1.0 absorbs floating-point artifacts and trace-melt days just above the 0.1
   mm/day noise floor.
3. **Snowmelt**: `rain_frac < MIXED_SPLIT`, where `MIXED_SPLIT` is the
   population-level median of `rain_frac` over all data-sufficient peaks with
   `rain_frac < 0.99` (mixed events), pooled across all 206 sites. This value
   was computed at run time as 0.2979.
4. **Rain-on-Snow**: `rain_frac >= MIXED_SPLIT` (after ruling out Rainfall).

The Snowmelt and Rain-on-Snow labels are operationally defined: they describe
position in the rain fraction distribution of mixed events, not direct physical
process attribution. Snowmelt-labelled peaks have relatively low rain fraction
within the mixed-event population; Rain-on-Snow-labelled peaks have relatively
higher rain fraction but still fall below the pure-rainfall threshold.

The rain fraction (2-class) variant is produced in Script 7 as a downstream
remap: Snowmelt and Rain-on-Snow peaks from the 3-class output are collapsed into
a single Non-Rainfall class, yielding two types (Rainfall, Non-Rainfall). The
2-class method provides a structural sensitivity check on whether the
Snowmelt/Rain-on-Snow split within the mixed-event pool drives meaningful
differences in upper-tail quantile estimates.

## 4.2 Decision Tree

```{r frac-thresh-flowchart, fig.cap = "Decision tree for the rain fraction (3-class) classification method (Script 6b). RAIN_FRAC_THRESH = 0.99 separates pure-rainfall events from mixed events. MIXED_SPLIT = 0.2979 is the population-level median rain fraction of mixed events across all 206 sites, computed at run time."}
gv_frac <- grViz("
digraph frac_thresh {

  graph [layout = dot, rankdir = TB, fontname = 'Helvetica', splines = polyline]
  node  [fontname = 'Helvetica', fontsize = 13, margin = 0.25]
  edge  [fontname = 'Helvetica', fontsize = 11]

  input [label = 'POT peak event\n(search_radius-day antecedent window)',
         shape = rectangle, style = filled, fillcolor = '#f0f0f0',
         width = 3.5, penwidth = 1.5]

  d1 [label = 'Complete WLDAS window?\nn_days_data >= 0.90 x search_radius',
      shape = diamond, style = filled, fillcolor = '#fef9c3',
      width = 4.2, height = 1.8, penwidth = 1.5, fixedsize = true]

  compute [label = 'Compute rain_frac\n(search_radius window, noise floor 0.1 mm/day)',
           shape = rectangle, style = filled, fillcolor = '#e8f4fd',
           width = 4.0, penwidth = 1.5]

  d2 [label = 'rain_frac defined?\n(total flux above noise floor > 0)',
      shape = diamond, style = filled, fillcolor = '#fef9c3',
      width = 4.2, height = 1.8, penwidth = 1.5, fixedsize = true]

  d3 [label = 'rain_frac >= 0.99?\n(RAIN_FRAC_THRESH)',
      shape = diamond, style = filled, fillcolor = '#fef9c3',
      width = 3.5, height = 1.6, penwidth = 1.5, fixedsize = true]

  d4 [label = 'rain_frac < 0.2979?\n(MIXED_SPLIT)',
      shape = diamond, style = filled, fillcolor = '#fef9c3',
      width = 3.5, height = 1.6, penwidth = 1.5, fixedsize = true]

  t_unc1 [label = 'Unclassified\n(no WLDAS)',
           shape = ellipse, style = filled, fillcolor = '#d9d9d9',
           width = 2.2, height = 0.9, penwidth = 1.5, fixedsize = true]

  t_unc2 [label = 'Unclassified\n(zero flux)',
           shape = ellipse, style = filled, fillcolor = '#d9d9d9',
           width = 2.2, height = 0.9, penwidth = 1.5, fixedsize = true]

  t_rain [label = 'Rainfall',
          shape = ellipse, style = filled, fillcolor = '#b2182b',
          fontcolor = 'white', width = 2.0, height = 0.9, penwidth = 1.5, fixedsize = true]

  t_snow [label = 'Snowmelt',
          shape = ellipse, style = filled, fillcolor = '#2166ac',
          fontcolor = 'white', width = 2.0, height = 0.9, penwidth = 1.5, fixedsize = true]

          shape = ellipse, style = filled, fillcolor = '#9970ab',
          fontcolor = 'white', width = 2.2, height = 0.9, penwidth = 1.5, fixedsize = true]

  input   -> d1
  d1      -> t_unc1   [taillabel = 'No',  labelangle = 45,  labeldistance = 2.5]
  d1      -> compute  [taillabel = 'Yes', labelangle = -45, labeldistance = 2.5]
  compute -> d2
  d2      -> t_unc2   [taillabel = 'No',  labelangle = 45,  labeldistance = 2.5]

  d4      -> t_ros    [taillabel = 'No',  labelangle = 45,  labeldistance = 2.5]
}
")

  ggplot2::guides(fill = ggplot2::guide_legend(
    override.aes = list(colour = NA)
  ))

ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "decision_space_frac_thresh.png"), width = 6.5, height = 4, units = "in")
```

Figure X. Fleet-wide distribution of `rain_frac` across all data-sufficient peak-over-threshold events (206 sites), colored by resulting flood type assignment. The dashed line at `RAIN_FRAC_THRESH = 0.99` separates pure-rainfall events (right) from mixed events. The dashed line at `MIXED_SPLIT = 0.2979` divides mixed events into Snowmelt (left) and Rain-on-Snow (right). The structural bimodality of the distribution — mass concentrated near 0 (melt-dominated) and near 1 (rainfall-dominated) — reflects the climatological separation of spring melt seasons from summer convective seasons at most Colorado sites.

## 4.3 Unclassified Events

Under the rain fraction method, a peak is Unclassified if fewer than 90% of its
`search_radius`-day antecedent window has WLDAS data, or if `rain_frac` is
undefined (zero total antecedent flux after noise-floor removal). Coverage
failures occur primarily at two margins: peaks predating the WLDAS archive and
rare partial windows at the temporal boundaries of the record. The fleet-wide
unclassified rate ranges from approximately 15–25% across sites at the median,
with the majority attributable to temporal coverage failures rather than
classification ambiguity. The coverage-failure fraction is concentrated at the
oldest sites with long records extending before the WLDAS archive start and is
not amenable to improvement through classification logic changes.

\newpage

# 5. Minimum Sample Size Thresholds and Single-Sample Alignment

Following Yu et al. (2022), the FFA pipeline applies two minimum sample size
thresholds: MIN_TYPE_SAMPLE = 20 (the minimum number of peaks of a given type
at a given site required to fit a per-type GPD) and MIN_SINGLE_SAMPLE = 25 (the
minimum number of peaks required to fit a single-population GPD). Sites falling
below MIN_SINGLE_SAMPLE are excluded from FFA entirely. Types falling below
MIN_TYPE_SAMPLE at a given site are demoted to Unclassified and excluded from
the per-type fits; the remaining types contribute to the mixture.

A key methodological decision concerns the ordering of the single-sample pool
selection relative to the MIN_TYPE_SAMPLE demotion step. The single-sample pool
consists of the top-$n$ peaks by discharge magnitude — one per water year up to
MIN_SINGLE_SAMPLE peaks — irrespective of flood type. Yu et al. (2022) describe
this pool as drawn from the full record before type-level filtering is applied.
This is the logically correct ordering: the single-sample pool is a superset
that should not depend on which types survive the MIN_TYPE_SAMPLE filter,
because its purpose is to represent the overall flood frequency at the site.

\newpage

# 6. FFA Fitting

## Distribution Family

Per-type flood frequency curves are fit using the Generalized Pareto Distribution
(GPD), following the L-moment estimation procedure of Yu et al. (2022). The
location parameter $\mu$ is fixed at the site-wide POT threshold (the median
daily maximum discharge), and the scale ($\sigma$) and shape ($\xi$) parameters
are estimated via L-moments using the `pargpa` function from the `lmomco` R
package. L-moment estimation is preferred over maximum likelihood for small
samples because it is unbiased and computationally robust.

The GP quantile function is:

$$Q(p) = \mu + \frac{\sigma}{\xi}\left[p^{-\xi} - 1\right]$$

where $p$ is the PoT exceedance probability. The PoT recurrence interval is
$RI = 1/p$, which corresponds to approximately the annual exceedance probability
when the PoT rate is near one event per year (as in Yu et al. 2022).

As a sensitivity check, the Log-Pearson Type III (LP3) distribution was also
implemented, fit to the log-transformed peaks via L-moments using the `parpe3`
function. The LP3 is the U.S. standard for annual peak flood frequency analysis
(Bulletin 17C) and provides a benchmark for comparison. Results from the LP3
sensitivity check are available in `ffa_params_lp3.rds` and
`ffa_quantiles_lp3.rds`.

## Mixture Survival Function

The mixture FFA follows Yu et al. (2022) Equation 3, in which the mixture
survival function is constructed as one minus the product of the per-type CDFs:

$$S_{\text{mix}}(x) = 1 - \prod_{k \in \mathcal{K}} F_k(x)$$

where $\mathcal{K}$ is the set of flood types with at least MIN_TYPE_SAMPLE
peaks at the site. The GPD CDF is $F_k(x) = 1 - [1 + \xi_k(x - \mu)/\sigma_k]^{-1/\xi_k}$.
The mixture recurrence interval at discharge level $x$ is
$RI_{\text{mix}}(x) = 1 / S_{\text{mix}}(x)$. Mixture quantiles at target return
periods are obtained by numerically inverting this relationship using `uniroot`.

## Data Sufficiency

Types with fewer than MIN_TYPE_SAMPLE events at a given site are excluded from
the mixture. Sites with fewer than MIN_SINGLE_SAMPLE total events across all
types are excluded from FFA entirely. These thresholds are identical to those
used by Yu et al. (2022) and were chosen to ensure that per-type GPD fits are
based on enough events to yield meaningful parameter estimates, particularly for
the shape parameter $\xi$, which governs upper-tail behavior.

```{r composition-figure, fig.height = 5.5, fig.cap = "Classification composition for the depth threshold and rain fraction (3-class) methods, showing the proportion of peaks assigned to each flood type using the pre-sample-size-filter (flood_type_raw) labels. 'Unclassified' in both methods reflects incomplete WLDAS coverage."}

# Build tidy labels for each method from the classified peaks directly.

label_dt <- peaks_dt %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    method     = "Depth",
    type_label = dplyr::case_when(
      as.character(flood_type_raw) == "rainfall"     ~ "Rainfall",
      as.character(flood_type_raw) == "snowmelt"     ~ "Snowmelt",
      as.character(flood_type_raw) == "rain_on_snow" ~ "Rain-on-Snow",
      TRUE                                           ~ "Unclassified"
    )
  ) %>%
  dplyr::select(method, type_label)

label_frac <- peaks_frac %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    method     = "Rain fraction (3-class)",
    type_label = dplyr::case_when(
      as.character(flood_type_raw) == "rainfall"     ~ "Rainfall",
      as.character(flood_type_raw) == "snowmelt"     ~ "Snowmelt",
      as.character(flood_type_raw) == "rain_on_snow" ~ "Rain-on-Snow",

    )
  ) %>%

comp_data <- dplyr::bind_rows(label_dt, label_frac) %>%
  dplyr::count(method, type_label) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(method) %>%

comp_colors <- c(

  "Rain-on-Snow" = "#9970ab",
  "Unclassified" = "#d9d9d9"
)

ggplot(comp_data, aes(x = method, y = pct, fill = type_label)) +
  geom_col(position = "stack", colour = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = comp_colors, name = "Flood type") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, name = "Fraction of all POT peaks") +

  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +

# 8. Temporal Trend Analysis

Flood hazard in Colorado is shaped by long-term changes in both climate
forcing and the relative frequency of different flood-generating processes.
To characterise these changes, two parallel trend analyses are carried out:
one targeting annual climate forcing variables at each site (Script 8) and
one targeting the annual frequency and composition of flood types classified
under the rain fraction scheme (Script 9). Both analyses use the
Mann-Kendall (MK) non-parametric test for monotonic trend and the Theil-Sen
slope estimator (median of all pairwise slopes). Tests are conducted at
$\alpha = 0.05$.

## 8.1 Approach

**Mann-Kendall and Theil-Sen.** The Mann-Kendall test ranks the time series
without assuming a particular distribution, making it robust to non-normality,
tied values, and the irregular gaps that arise from gauge record gaps.
The Theil-Sen slope estimator is correspondingly resistant to outliers because
it is based on the median rather than the mean of pairwise slopes. Both are
widely used for hydrological trend detection (e.g.\ Helsel & Hirsch 2002; Yue
et al.\ 2002).

**Significance threshold.** Under a true null of no trend, exactly 5% of MK
tests are expected to return $p < 0.05$ by chance. Throughout this section,
a dashed reference line is drawn at this expected rate to distinguish systematic
evidence from random inflation of rejections.

**Climate forcing variables** (Script 8). Trends are tested for five annual
series at each site: total precipitation ($\mathrm{mm}$), peak SWE
($\mathrm{mm}$), maximum peak discharge ($\mathrm{cfs}$), POT event rate
(events per year), and median rain fraction of POT events (dimensionless). A
minimum of 20 non-missing years is required for the MK test to have adequate
power (Yue et al.\ 2002). Water years with WLDAS day coverage below 90% of
expected are excluded from precipitation and SWE series before testing to
avoid bias from incomplete records.

**Flood type frequency variables** (Script 9, rain fraction 3-class). Trends
are tested separately for each flood type (Rainfall, Snowmelt, Rain-on-Snow)
in two metrics: annual count (events per year) and annual proportion (fraction
of all classified peaks). Site eligibility requires $\geq 20$ water years with
at least one classified peak and $\geq 5$ years with at least one peak of the
specific type being tested. Both metrics are informative: count trends detect
absolute changes in occurrence rate, while proportion trends detect composition
shifts independent of the total peak rate.

## 8.2 Climate Forcing Trends

```{r climate-trend-summary, fig.height=4, fig.width=7}
MK_ALPHA_REPORT <- 0.05

VAR_LABELS_REPORT <- c(
  total_precip_mm        = "Total annual\nprecipitation",
  peak_swe_mm            = "Peak SWE",
  max_peak_discharge_cfs = "Max peak\ndischarge",
  pot_event_rate         = "POT event rate",
  median_rain_frac       = "Median rain\nfraction of POT events"
)

# Variable order: arrange roughly from precipitation inputs to hydrologic outputs
VAR_ORDER <- c("total_precip_mm", "peak_swe_mm", "median_rain_frac",
               "pot_event_rate", "max_peak_discharge_cfs")

clim_sum <- climate_trends %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    significant = !is.na(p_value) & p_value < MK_ALPHA_REPORT,
    direction   = dplyr::case_when(
      significant & sen_slope > 0 ~ "Increasing",
      significant & sen_slope < 0 ~ "Decreasing",
      TRUE                        ~ "Not significant"
    )
  ) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(variable) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(
    n_total = dplyr::n(),
    n_pos   = sum(direction == "Increasing"),
    n_neg   = sum(direction == "Decreasing"),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    var_label  = VAR_LABELS_REPORT[variable],
    var_label  = factor(var_label, levels = VAR_LABELS_REPORT[VAR_ORDER]),
    null_count = round(0.05 * n_total)
  )

clim_plot_df <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  dplyr::transmute(clim_sum, var_label, direction = "Increasing",  n =  n_pos),
  dplyr::transmute(clim_sum, var_label, direction = "Decreasing",  n = -n_neg)
)

null_line <- round(0.05 * dplyr::first(clim_sum$n_total))

ggplot2::ggplot(clim_plot_df,
                ggplot2::aes(x = n, y = var_label, fill = direction)) +
  ggplot2::geom_col(width = 0.6, alpha = 0.9) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = c(-null_line, null_line),
                      linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey35", linewidth = 0.7) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey20", linewidth = 0.4) +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("Increasing" = "#b2182b", "Decreasing" = "#2166ac"),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(
    name   = "Number of sites with significant trend",
    labels = function(x) abs(x),
    breaks = c(-40, -30, -20, -10, 0, 10, 20, 30, 40)
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_discrete(name = NULL) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title    = "Climate forcing trends across all eligible sites",
    subtitle = sprintf(
      "Dashed lines: expected 5%% significant by chance (~%d sites)  |  α = %.2f",
      null_line, MK_ALPHA_REPORT
    )
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
  ggplot2::theme(
    legend.position  = "bottom",
    panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = ggplot2::element_blank()
  )

ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "climate_forcing_trends.png"), width = 6.5, height = 4, units = "in")

```

Total precipitation shows the most widespread significant trends, with more
sites exhibiting decreasing than increasing totals. Peak SWE trends are more
evenly split, with a modest excess of increasing trends — plausibly reflecting
recent high-snowpack years within some longer records rather than a sustained
directional shift. The POT event rate shows exclusively decreasing significant
trends, consistent with a contraction of flood-generating conditions at some
sites. Max peak discharge trends are weak and nearly balanced, and median rain
fraction shows slightly more sites with decreasing than increasing values.
For all five variables, the fraction of sites with significant trends is small
relative to the total, and in most cases does not substantially exceed the
expected false-positive rate — evidence that large-scale, coherent trends in
Colorado flood climate remain difficult to detect at individual sites across
the historical record length.

## 8.3 Flood Type Frequency Trends

The following figure shows, for each flood type and metric, the percentage of
eligible sites with a significant Mann-Kendall trend, split by direction. Only
the rain fraction (3-class) classification is shown; depth threshold results
follow the same pattern. Sites with fewer than 20 classified years or fewer
than 5 years of the specific type are excluded from the eligible pool for that
type.

```{r fft-trend-summary, fig.height=4, fig.width=7}
TYPE_LABELS_REPORT <- c(
  rainfall     = "Rainfall",
  snowmelt     = "Snowmelt",
  rain_on_snow = "Rain-on-Snow"
)

fft_agg <- fft_trends$aggregate %>%
  dplyr::filter(population == "all_eligible") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    type_label   = factor(TYPE_LABELS_REPORT[flood_type],
                          levels = c("Rain-on-Snow", "Snowmelt", "Rainfall")),
    metric_label = dplyr::recode(metric,
                                 count      = "Count (events / yr)",
                                 proportion = "Proportion (fraction / yr)")
  )

fft_plot_df <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  dplyr::transmute(fft_agg, type_label, metric_label,
                   direction = "Increasing", pct =  pct_sig_pos),
  dplyr::transmute(fft_agg, type_label, metric_label,
                   direction = "Decreasing", pct = -pct_sig_neg)
)

x_lim <- 20

ggplot2::ggplot(fft_plot_df,
                ggplot2::aes(x = pct, y = type_label, fill = direction)) +
  ggplot2::geom_col(width = 0.6, alpha = 0.9) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = c(-5, 5),
                      linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey35", linewidth = 0.7) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey20", linewidth = 0.4) +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("Increasing" = "#b2182b", "Decreasing" = "#2166ac"),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(
    name   = "Sites with significant trend (% of eligible)",
    labels = function(x) paste0(abs(x), "%"),
    limits = c(-x_lim, x_lim)
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_discrete(name = NULL) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~metric_label, ncol = 2) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title    = "Flood type frequency trends — Rain fraction (3-class)",
    subtitle = sprintf(
      "Dashed lines: expected 5%% significant by chance  |  α = %.2f",
      MK_ALPHA_REPORT
    )
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
  ggplot2::theme(
    legend.position    = "bottom",
    panel.grid.minor   = ggplot2::element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = ggplot2::element_blank(),
    strip.background   = ggplot2::element_rect(fill = "grey92", colour = NA)
  )

ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "flood_frequency_trends.png"), width = 6.5, height = 4, units = "in")
```

Across all three flood types and both metrics, the proportion of sites with
significant trends is broadly consistent with the expected false-positive rate.
The clearest exception is Snowmelt proportion in the unregulated sub-population,
where approximately 14% of eligible sites show a significant trend — roughly
twice the expected rate — with the majority of those being increases. This is
counterintuitive given broader evidence of declining snowmelt contributions in
the western US, but may reflect the relatively short period of record at some
sites, inter-decadal variability, or the operational definition of Snowmelt
under the rain fraction scheme (below-median rain fraction of mixed events)
rather than a physically consistent process label. Rainfall proportion shows a
modest excess of significant trends across both count and proportion metrics,
with slightly more sites exhibiting decreases than increases, consistent with a
gradual shift in the balance of event types at some locations.

\newpage

# 9. Limitations and Future Work

**WLDAS spatial resolution.** WLDAS operates at approximately 12.5 km
grid spacing across CONUS. Colorado's complex mountain terrain features
elevation gradients of hundreds of meters per kilometer, and basin-averaged
values at this resolution mask important sub-basin variability in snowmelt
timing, rainfall intensity, and frozen-soil infiltration capacity. The
classification is therefore an approximation based on spatially smoothed
forcing, and threshold values derived from the fleet-wide rain fraction
distribution reflect patterns in the smoothed rather than the point-scale signal.

**Daily versus instantaneous peak flows.** The analysis uses the maximum daily
discharge within each POT event, whereas the physical flood peak is
instantaneous. For small basins with short concentration times, the daily
maximum may substantially underestimate the true peak. Yu et al. (2022) note
that the mixture effect — the departure of the mixture quantile curve from a
single-population fit — is likely stronger at the instantaneous scale, where
within-type variability is lower and between-type differences more pronounced.
The daily-aggregated results reported here should therefore be interpreted as a
conservative estimate of the mixture effect.

**Rain-on-Snow viability.** At sites where fewer than MIN_TYPE_SAMPLE
rain-on-snow events are identified, the rain-on-snow component is excluded from
the mixture and its contribution is implicitly absorbed into the remaining types.
Rain-on-snow viability is lowest at very high elevations (where rainfall in the
antecedent window is rare) and at very low elevations (where seasonal snowpack is
absent). Under the rain fraction (3-class) method, 96 sites have sufficient
rain-on-snow samples and are predominantly at mid to upper-mid elevations. Future
work could explore whether a relaxed MIN_TYPE_SAMPLE (e.g., 10–15) would
meaningfully expand the viable rain-on-snow set without destabilizing parameter
estimates.

**Climate nonstationarity.** The analysis treats all years of record as equally
representative of current flood hazard. Evidence from the broader literature
suggests that snowmelt-driven flood magnitudes have declined in the western US
as temperatures have risen, while extreme rainfall events have increased. The
fitted distributions therefore represent a mixture of historical conditions
rather than a stationary representation of current or future hazard. Nonstationary
FFA methods incorporating climate covariates would be a natural extension.

**Higher-resolution land surface model output.** The Basin Characterization Model
(BCM) and similar products provide spatially distributed runoff estimates at finer
resolution than WLDAS. A comparison of WLDAS-based classifications with BCM-based
classifications at a subset of sites would help characterize the sensitivity of
the mixture FFA results to the choice of land surface forcing product.
